meta.description: Not Jefferson. The line's earliest known print appearance is 1986, in a book by a pseudonymous "John Galt" that credits him with no source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The democracy will cease to exist when you take away from those who are willing to work and give to those who would not'?
meta.ogDescription: Monticello and Wikiquote both call it spurious — earliest print 1986. Here's what Jefferson actually wrote about taxing industry, in 1816.

answer.label: Not Thomas Jefferson — a modern fabrication
answer.sourceLine: No such sentence appears anywhere in Thomas Jefferson’s writings. Its earliest known appearance in print is 1986 — a book issued under the pseudonym “John Galt” that credits the line to Jefferson but gives no source — and the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, having searched the Founders Online corpus, the retirement papers and the major newspaper and book databases, records no earlier trace, no variations, and no other attributions.

source.heading: The closest thing Jefferson actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Not found in any writing of Thomas Jefferson
Addition to Note for Destutt de Tracy’s Treatise on Political Economy

source.excerpt: To this a single observation shall yet be added. Whether property alone, and the whole of what each citizen possesses, shall be subject to contribution, or only it’s surplus after satisfying his first wants, or whether the faculties of body and mind shall contribute also from their annual earnings, is a question to be decided. but, when decided, and the principle settled, it is to be equally and fairly applied to all. to take from one, because it is thought that his own industry and that of his father[s] has acquired too much, in order to spare to others, who, or whose fathers have not exercised equal industry and skill, is to violate arbitrarily the first principle of association, ‘the guarantee to every one of a free exercise of his industry, & the fruits acquired by it.’ if the overgrown wealth of an individual be deemed dangerous to the state, the best corrective is the law of equal inheritance to all in equal degree: and the better as this enforces a law of nature, while extra-taxation violates one.
trail: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation’s Thomas Jefferson Encyclopedia ↗ files this line under Spurious Quotations. Its status line is unambiguous: “This exact quotation has not been found in any of the writings of Thomas Jefferson.” The entry, by reference librarian Anna Berkes, records the earliest known appearance in print as 1986, with no known variations and no other attributions.

That 1986 appearance is page 312 of Dreams Come Due: Government and Economics as if Freedom Mattered (New York: Simon & Schuster, 1986). Publishers Weekly’s review ↗ confirms the publisher and extent and notes the author wrote under a pseudonym borrowed “from the hero of Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged.” The book credits Jefferson but prints no citation.

Wikiquote’s Thomas Jefferson page ↗ independently places the line in its Misattributed section, citing the same book and the same page 312, and concluding it “is not found anywhere in his works.” Quote Investigator has no entry on this quotation.

The nearest genuine text is Jefferson’s addition to his note for Destutt de Tracy’s Treatise on Political Economy, transcribed at Founders Online ↗ from the manuscript at the Library of Congress (DLC: TJ Papers, 206:36788). It was enclosed in Jefferson’s 18 May 1816 letter to Joseph Milligan — and, the editors note, was never printed with his note in the published Treatise.
source.excerptNote: This is not the quotation in question — it is the genuine Jefferson passage that Monticello says the fake bears “a very vague resemblance” to. Note what is missing: no democracy, no ceasing to exist, no unwilling workers. Jefferson’s lowercase spelling and ampersand are preserved from the manuscript transcription.

sourceLink.text: Read the full 1816 addition at Jefferson Quotes & Family Letters

source.rightsNote: Rights on the popular line cannot be settled, because its authorship cannot be: it is a fabrication with no identified originator, presented without a source in its earliest known printing ↗ — a 1986 Simon & Schuster book that is itself in copyright. The genuine Jefferson passage excerpted above is a separate matter and is firmly in the public domain: he wrote it around 18 May 1816, and it was published in the scholarly record long before 1931.

author.metaLine: 1743–1826 · Third U.S. president and author of the Declaration of Independence
author.bio: Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence, served as the third president of the United States, and founded the University of Virginia. He wrote voluminously — some 19,000 letters survive — which is precisely why fabricated quotations are so easy to test against him: the corpus is searchable, and this line simply is not in it. Jefferson did write about the justice of taxing acquired industry, but in language far more careful and conditional than the slogan now sold on his behalf.

misattribution.heading: How a 1986 slogan became a Founding Father's warning
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook manufactured quotation: it enters the record fully formed, in one modern book, credited to a long-dead statesman with no citation attached — and then travels on the strength of the name alone.

items.why: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation’s Thomas Jefferson Encyclopedia ↗ states that “this exact quotation has not been found in any of the writings of Thomas Jefferson,” and records “Variations: None known” and “Other attributions: None known” — the profile of a line that was minted once and copied ever since, rather than one that evolved in circulation.

Monticello traces the line to page 312 of Dreams Come Due: Government and Economics as if Freedom Mattered (New York: Simon & Schuster, 1986), where it is credited to Jefferson but carries no citation. Publishers Weekly’s 1986 review ↗ notes that the author borrowed the pseudonym from the hero of Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged. Because that book presents the line as Jefferson’s rather than claiming it, the true originator remains unknown — 1986 is the earliest documented trace, not a proven moment of coinage.
Wikiquote’s Jefferson page ↗ reaches the same verdict from the same evidence, placing the line in its Misattributed section and noting it “is not found anywhere in his works.”

Monticello’s researchers searched Founders Online, the Jefferson retirement papers, Google Books, Google Scholar, the Internet Archive, America’s Historical Newspapers, Early American Imprints, Eighteenth Century Collections Online, 19th Century U.S. Newspapers, American Periodicals Series Online and JSTOR — a corpus that would readily surface a Jefferson sentence quoted between 1826 and 1986. As the Fake History project puts it ↗, it is “a modern fake, first seen in 1986.” A 160-year silence is not an archival gap; it is an absence.

misattribution.truthLine: Jefferson did write about taxing one man’s industry to relieve another — around 18 May 1816, in an addition to his note for Destutt de Tracy’s Treatise on Political Economy ↗. But Monticello calls the resemblance “very vague,” and for good reason: Jefferson never mentions democracy ceasing to exist, and he closes by proposing equal inheritance as the best corrective to overgrown wealth.

context.heading: A slogan Jefferson never reached for
lead: The line has an obvious appeal: it compresses an entire argument about welfare and taxation into one balanced, quotable sentence and stamps it with the authority of the man who wrote the Declaration of Independence. That combination — ideologically useful, rhetorically tidy, conveniently unfalsifiable — is the signature of a manufactured quotation. Jefferson is among the most heavily indexed writers in American history; a sentence this pointed would not have hidden until 1986.

What makes the fake instructive is how much weaker it is than the real thing. Jefferson genuinely did write about the injustice of taxing one man’s accumulated industry to relieve another, in an addition to a note ↗ he drafted around 18 May 1816 for his edition of Destutt de Tracy’s Treatise on Political Economy. But his actual sentence is hedged, conditional, and ends somewhere the slogan’s admirers rarely quote: with Jefferson recommending equal inheritance as the proper corrective to dangerous concentrations of wealth.
detailsBody: Monticello’s researchers are careful to note that the fake bears only a “very vague resemblance” to Jefferson’s 1816 remark. The two are not paraphrases of one another. Jefferson is arguing a narrow point about how the principle of taxation, once settled, must be “equally and fairly applied to all” — not making a prophecy about democracy collapsing, a word and a claim that appear nowhere in his passage.

There is a further irony in the manuscript record. Jefferson’s addition was enclosed in a letter to his publisher Joseph Milligan on 18 May 1816, and despite Milligan’s assurance that it would run, Founders Online records that the addition “was not printed with TJ’s note on page 202” of the published Treatise. The genuine sentence on this theme was never even published in the book it was written for — while the counterfeit has circulated on posters, chain emails and merchandise for four decades.
context.pull: Jefferson’s real passage ends by endorsing equal inheritance as a law of nature — the part the slogan leaves out.
